papers.title: Integrative therapies for symptom management in dementia from a palliative perspective: narrative review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
papers.abstract: Dementia affects over 55 million people worldwide, with behavioral and psychological symptoms (BPSD) impacting over 90% of individuals. Conventional pharmacotherapies offer limited benefits with substantial side effects. Integrative care therapies (ICT) represent a complementary approach, yet the evidence supporting their use has been largely absent from the palliative care literature. This narrative review synthesizes ICT systematic reviews and meta-analyses to bridge this gap. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library were searched for systematic reviews and meta-analyses published between 2015 and June 2026 evaluating ICT for dementia symptom management. Seminal earlier works were also included when updated reviews were unavailable. Individual randomized controlled trials (RCTs), validation studies, and non-English publications were excluded, except selected sources cited for mechanistic, safety, regulatory, or pivotal-trial context. Cognitive stimulation achieved the highest evidence certainty, with high-certainty evidence for communication and social interaction and moderate-certainty evidence for cognition, quality of life (QOL), and challenging behaviors. Music therapy showed moderate-certainty evidence for depression improvement but not agitation. Light therapy and movement-based mind-body therapies (MBT) demonstrated benefit across the broadest range of domains-including cognition, BPSD, and sleep-though certainty remained low-to-very-low. Massage and aromatherapy showed consistent short-term benefits for agitation and depression. Acupuncture augmented conventional medication for improvement in cognition and activities of daily living (ADL). Dietary and herbal therapies contributed primarily to cognitive domains, with Ginkgo biloba showing the most robust BPSD evidence. Cannabinoids showed preliminary evidence for agitation and in severe disease. Across modalities, effects were often limited to the treatment period, early-stage disease showed the most robust benefits, and safety profiles were favorable. Only cognitive stimulation and music therapy achieved moderate or higher Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) ratings. Multiple ICT modalities show promising evidence for dementia symptom management that aligns with palliative care principles, though most evidence is of low-to-very-low certainty. Future research should prioritize pragmatic trials in hospice and palliative care settings using outcomes meaningful to this context, including comfort, caregiver experience, and healthcare utilization.

papers.title: The interplay of exercise, immunity, and suboptimal health in college students: an integrative narrative review with public health implications.
papers.abstract: The immune system, vital for pathogen defense and tissue repair, is strongly influenced by lifestyle. With declining physical activity and rising chronic disease burdens, the role of exercise in modulating immunity has drawn growing attention. College students, undergoing critical life transitions, are susceptible to lifestyle-related risks such as sedentary behavior, insufficient sleep, and high psychological stress, which often lead to suboptimal health status. Immune and inflammatory risks are a concern among college students: prolonged sedentary behavior, chronic sleep deprivation, and elevated psychological stress frequently co-occur. Each of these behaviors is associated with low-grade inflammation and altered immune regulation in adults, and their clustering in students is therefore a reasonable basis for concern, although the strength of the association with immune outcomes has seldom been measured directly in this group. The term suboptimal health status is used in this review as a self-reported functional syndrome, defined in Section 3.4, rather than as an established clinical entity. We examine the effects of different physical activities on immune function, chronic low-grade inflammation, and suboptimal health status in college students, outlining the basic framework of exercise immunology and distinguishing acute from chronic exercise responses. Evidence is categorized by exercise type, including moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, high-intensity training, resistance training, and mind-body practices, and their mechanisms, such as myokine-mediated anti-inflammatory signaling, immune cell mobilization, fat loss, and the mediation of sleep and emotion, are summarized. We critically discuss the methodological challenges in this field, separating two sources of disagreement that are often conflated: study design, which determines the causal question a study can answer, and measurement method, which determines how accurately exposure and outcome are captured. We analyze the limitations of each, including the inability of cross-sectional studies to establish causality, measurement bias in self-reported data, and ecological validity and compliance issues in trials, and we note how the same distinction applies to outcome assessment, from self-reported symptoms to immune-cell, cytokine, and clinical infection measures. Notable gaps are identified, including the "population mismatch" whereby findings from other populations are extrapolated to college students, limitations in sample selection and measurement standardization, and the lack of individualized and comprehensive intervention studies. This narrative review underscores the importance of understanding the relationship between exercise and immunity in college students, provides an overview of current knowledge, identifies critical limitations, and proposes future directions. Evidence was assembled through a structured narrative search, and findings obtained directly in college students are distinguished throughout from those extrapolated from athletic or clinical populations. It also offers public health implications for Chinese university settings, emphasizing targeted health education, campus-wide exercise interventions, sedentary behavior reduction, and integrated sleep and stress management to promote student wellbeing.

papers.title: Prevalence and factors associated with sleep deprivation in nursing technicians working in shifts.

papers.title: Reversal of photoperiodic flowering in temperate grasses rewired light inputs and floral outputs of the circadian clock.
papers.abstract: The transition from long-day (LD) to short-day (SD) flowering enabled temperate grasses of the tribe Stipeae (Poaceae: Pooideae) to colonise neotropical montane habitats, yet the transcriptomic basis of this shift remains poorly understood. Here, we used comparative transcriptomics and functional principal component analysis to examine diel gene expression in SD-flowering Nassella pubiflora and LD-flowering Oloptum miliaceum. Although photoperiod substantially rewired the diel transcriptome in both species, interspecific expression differences were limited to a small subset of orthologous genes. Divergence was most pronounced under SDs and involved floral integrators, light-signalling genes, and circadian clock targets, while core circadian clock gene expression remained largely conserved. These results suggest that the reversal from LD to SD flowering in Stipeae involved modifications to relatively few but central flowering pathway genes that convey photoperiod signals, rather than widespread changes to the endogenous timekeeping system. Our findings provide insight into the genetic architecture underlying niche transitions and photoperiod responsiveness in grasses and identify candidate genes that could potentially be targeted to optimise flowering time in cereal crops.
